## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Computational Statistics
  Official title       Computational Statistics
  Instructors          S.ALLASSONNIERE (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 1 · period 1 (28/09/2026 – 08/01/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 40 h (lectures 20 h, labs 20 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Learning]{.badge .label}[Track Santé]{.badge .track}
  Language             Not displayed (the master-mva.com description is written in English)
  Assessment           master-mva.com: homework following each training session (4 assignments) = 2/3 of the grade; oral presentation of one scientific paper, team work (“Team work (2)”), no report = 1/3 · Université Paris-Saclay: “Evaluation Continue non Intégrale” (continuous assessment that is not the only component of the grade)
  Prerequisites        Not displayed (neither on master-mva.com nor on the Université Paris-Saclay course detail)
  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: an M2 student with a solid M1 in probability and optimisation who must fit models with hidden variables, compute Bayesian estimators, or sample from a distribution known only up to a constant.

**Empirical first**: EM fitted to a two-component Gaussian mixture raises its likelihood at every iteration, yet is still moving after 200 iterations (ch. 3). A random-walk Metropolis chain started in one mode of a bimodal target never visits the other mode in 20 000 steps (ch. 8). The course explains both behaviours, and then repairs them.

The course is about the algorithms that turn a statistical model into numbers: stochastic gradients, EM and its stochastic versions, stochastic approximation, simulation and Markov chain Monte Carlo, and likelihood-free inference. It shares tools with [Convex Optimization and Applications in Machine Learning](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html), [Introduction to Probabilistic Graphical Models and Deep Generative Models](../s1-probabilistic-graphical-models/index.html) and [Stochastic Calculus in Machine Learning](../s1-stochastic-calculus-ml/index.html), and it prepares [Bayesian Machine Learning](../s2-bayesian-ml/index.html) and [Biostatistics](../s2-biostatistics/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Prove the convergence rates of the stochastic gradient algorithm, and diagnose its step-size and conditioning bottlenecks.
-   Write a posterior distribution, derive Bayes estimators for standard losses, and identify which integral makes a Bayesian computation hard.
-   Derive EM for a latent-variable model, prove that it increases the likelihood, and predict its speed from the fraction of missing information.
-   Recognise a Majorize–Minimize algorithm and build a surrogate for a new objective.
-   Prove the almost-sure convergence of a Robbins–Monro algorithm, and choose step sizes and averaging to reach the optimal variance.
-   Simulate random variables by inversion, transformation and rejection, and design an importance-sampling estimator for a rare event.
-   Implement Metropolis–Hastings and Gibbs samplers, prove their invariance, and assess them with autocorrelations, effective sample sizes and several chains.
-   Implement SAEM and MCMC-SAEM, and explain why one simulation per iteration suffices.
-   Tune a sampler by adaptive MCMC without destroying its ergodicity, and sample multimodal targets with parallel tempering.
-   Perform approximate Bayesian computation, and choose its tolerance and summary statistics knowingly.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com states that the course details statistical computational methods and Bayesian inference. It starts with the stochastic gradient algorithm, its theoretical properties and its numerical bottlenecks. After a brief introduction to Bayesian inference, it discusses the numerical challenges of computing Bayesian estimators, which lead to the EM algorithm, its stochastic versions and, more generally, Majorize–Minimize algorithms.

Stochastic approximation is then detailed, to understand the convergence conditions of these algorithms. The second part is devoted to the simulation of random variables: from the rejection method to the classical MCMC samplers (Metropolis–Hastings and Gibbs), then recent advances in MCMC: adaptive MCMC, adaptive parallel tempering and approximate Bayesian computation. The description announces 20 h of lectures and 20 h of training and lab sessions, and lists the course for the Master 2 MVA and Data Science.

### Where this course fits in the programme

Official prerequisites: not displayed. The material assumes M1 probability (conditional expectation, laws of large numbers, central limit theorem, finite Markov chains), M1 optimisation (gradients, convexity) and fluent NumPy.

-   **Preparation** — the refreshers [Probability and Statistics for MVA](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html), [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization for MVA](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) and [Scientific Python, NumPy and PyTorch for MVA](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html); ch. 0 restates what this course uses.
-   **Related courses in semester 1** — [Convex Optimization and Applications in Machine Learning](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html) (deterministic counterpart of ch. 1), [Introduction to Probabilistic Graphical Models and Deep Generative Models](../s1-probabilistic-graphical-models/index.html) (EM and variational inference), [Stochastic Calculus in Machine Learning](../s1-stochastic-calculus-ml/index.html) (Langevin sampling, ch. 10), [Introduction to Statistical Learning](../s1-intro-statistical-learning/index.html) and, in the Santé track, [Medical Image Analysis Based on Generative, Geometric and Biophysical Models](../s1-medical-image-analysis/index.html).
-   **Courses that build on it in semester 2** — [Bayesian Machine Learning](../s2-bayesian-ml/index.html), [Inverse Problems and Imaging: Statistical and Stochastic Approaches](../s2-inverse-problems-imaging/index.html), [Biostatistics](../s2-biostatistics/index.html) (mixed-effects models, ch. 7), [Reinforcement Learning](../s2-reinforcement-learning/index.html) and [Sequential Learning](../s2-sequential-learning/index.html) (stochastic approximation, ch. 4), [Graphical Models: Discrete Inference and Learning](../s2-graphical-models-discrete/index.html) (Gibbs sampling), [Diffusion and Multiscale Models in Artificial Intelligence](../s2-diffusion-multiscale/index.html) (Langevin dynamics, ch. 10).

### Course outline

-   **0. Review: Monte Carlo, convexity and martingales** — the Monte Carlo error bar, Kullback–Leibler divergence, exponential families, smooth and strongly convex functions, martingale convergence.
-   **1. The stochastic gradient algorithm** — unbiased gradients, rates in the strongly convex and convex cases, and the numerical bottlenecks.
-   **2. Bayesian inference and its computational challenges** — posterior, Bayes estimators, large-sample behaviour, and the integrals that make everything hard.
-   **3. Majorize–Minimize and the EM algorithm** — surrogate optimisation, EM as its probabilistic instance, Gaussian mixtures, convergence and speed.
-   **4. Stochastic approximation** — Robbins–Monro, the Robbins–Siegmund lemma, almost-sure convergence, the ODE method, rates and averaging.
-   **5. Simulation of random variables** — inversion, transformations, rejection and importance sampling.
-   **6. Markov chain Monte Carlo: Metropolis–Hastings and Gibbs** — invariance, ergodicity, the two classical samplers and their diagnostics.
-   **7. Stochastic versions of EM** — MCEM, SEM, SAEM and MCMC-SAEM, with the Lyapunov argument behind SAEM.
-   **8. Adaptive MCMC and parallel tempering** — learning the proposal, when adaptation is safe, crossing energy barriers with a temperature ladder.
-   **9. Approximate Bayesian computation** — inference by simulation, tolerance and summary statistics, ABC-MCMC and ABC-SMC.
-   **10. Research directions and open problems** — gradient-based samplers, Markovian stochastic approximation, theory of EM, simulation-based inference (self-study).

### How to study this module

-   Read ch. 0 before the first session, even if the tools look familiar: the later proofs cite its numbered results without restating them.
-   After each lecture, redo the proofs of the boxed theorems without notes; the written-exam proposal asks for exactly these arguments.
-   Run every code block of a chapter during its lab, then change one parameter (step size, proposal scale, tolerance) and predict the effect before running again.
-   Do the exercises listed in the *Practice* column right after the matching session; the ★★★ exercises are good preparation for the paper presentation.
-   Python environment: NumPy and SciPy only for the course code; every block fixes its random seed and runs in under 30 seconds on a laptop.

## 0. Review: Monte Carlo, convexity and martingales {#ch0}

Every algorithm of the course is analysed with four M1 tools. The law of large numbers and the central limit theorem give Monte Carlo its error bar. The Kullback–Leibler divergence makes EM work. Smooth and strongly convex functions make gradient methods converge. Martingales make stochastic approximation converge.

This chapter states each tool in the form used later, with short proofs. Background is in the refreshers [Probability and Statistics](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) and [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html).

### 0.1 Monte Carlo integration

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Monte Carlo estimator]{.tag} Let $\pi$ be a probability distribution and $h$ a function with $\pi(h^2) < \infty$, where $\pi(h) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[h(X)]$. For $X_1, \dots, X_n$ independent with law $\pi$, the Monte Carlo estimator is
$$
\hat I_n = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n h(X_i), \qquad \mathbb{E}[\hat I_n] = \pi(h), \qquad \mathrm{Var}(\hat I_n) = \frac{\sigma_h^2}{n},
$$
with $\sigma_h^2 = \mathrm{Var}_\pi(h(X))$.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — The Monte Carlo error bar]{.tag} By the strong law of large numbers, $\hat I_n \to \pi(h)$ almost surely. By the central limit theorem, $\sqrt n\,(\hat I_n - \pi(h))$ converges in law to $\mathcal N(0, \sigma_h^2)$.

With $\hat\sigma_n$ the empirical standard deviation of the $h(X_i)$, an asymptotic 95 % confidence interval is
$$
\hat I_n \pm 1.96\, \frac{\hat\sigma_n}{\sqrt n}.
$$

The rate $n^{-1/2}$ does not depend on the dimension of $X$; the constant $\sigma_h$ does.

By contrast, a tensor-product quadrature rule of order $r$ with $m$ nodes per axis uses $N = m^d$ evaluations. Its error is of order $N^{-r/d}$, which degrades with the dimension.
:::

::: ex
[Example 0.3 — Monte Carlo in dimension d]{.tag} Take $X \sim \mathcal N(0, I_d)$ and $h(x) = \exp(-\|x\|^2/2)$.

-   Since $\mathbb{E}[e^{-tZ^2}] = (1 + 2t)^{-1/2}$ for $Z \sim \mathcal N(0,1)$, independence gives $\pi(h) = 2^{-d/2}$ and $\pi(h^2) = 3^{-d/2}$.
-   The relative variance per sample is therefore
    $$
    \frac{\sigma_h^2}{\pi(h)^2} = \Big(\frac43\Big)^{d/2} - 1 .
    $$
-   For $d = 10$ this is $3.21$, so $n = 10^5$ samples give a relative standard error of $\sqrt{3.21/10^5} \approx 0.0057$.
-   For $d = 50$ it is $1328$, and the relative standard error becomes $0.115$.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 100_000
for d in [1, 10, 50]:
    X = rng.standard_normal((n, d))
    h = np.exp(-0.5 * (X ** 2).sum(axis=1))      # h(x) = exp(-|x|^2 / 2)
    est = h.mean()
    se = h.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n)              # CLT standard error
    exact = 2.0 ** (-d / 2)
    print(f"d={d:2d}  estimate={est:.4e}  exact={exact:.4e}  relative s.e.={se / est:.4f}")
```

The run prints relative standard errors of 0.0012, 0.0057 and 0.133. The rate is the same in every dimension; the constant explodes because the few samples near the origin carry all the mass of $h$. Importance sampling (ch. 5.4) and MCMC (ch. 6) are two ways of attacking that constant.
:::

### 0.2 Jensen's inequality and the Kullback–Leibler divergence

::: def
[Definition 0.4 — Kullback–Leibler divergence]{.tag} For two densities $q$ and $p$ with $q = 0$ wherever $p = 0$,
$$
\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p) = \int q(z) \log \frac{q(z)}{p(z)}\, dz .
$$
It is not symmetric in $(q, p)$ and is not a distance, but it measures how much $q$ differs from $p$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.5 — Gibbs' inequality]{.tag} For all densities $q$ and $p$,
$$
\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p) \ge 0,
$$
with equality if and only if $q = p$ almost everywhere.

::: proof
The logarithm is strictly concave, so Jensen's inequality under $q$ gives
$$
-\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p) = \mathbb{E}_q\Big[\log \frac{p(Z)}{q(Z)}\Big] \le \log \mathbb{E}_q\Big[\frac{p(Z)}{q(Z)}\Big] \le \log 1 = 0 .
$$
Equality in Jensen's inequality forces $p/q$ to be constant $q$-almost surely, and the constant is 1 because both densities integrate to 1. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

This inequality is the whole reason EM increases the likelihood (Theorem 3.6).

### 0.3 Exponential families

::: def
[Definition 0.6 — Exponential family]{.tag} A family of densities is an exponential family with natural parameter $\eta \in \mathbb{R}^q$ and sufficient statistic $S(x) \in \mathbb{R}^q$ if
$$
p(x; \eta) = h(x) \exp\big(\langle \eta, S(x) \rangle - A(\eta)\big), \qquad A(\eta) = \log \int h(x)\, e^{\langle \eta, S(x)\rangle}\, dx .
$$
Examples: the Gaussian $\mathcal N(m, \sigma^2)$ with $S(x) = (x, x^2)$; the Bernoulli and Poisson laws with $S(x) = x$; a categorical law with $S(x)$ the vector of indicators.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.7 — The log-partition function]{.tag} In the interior of the natural parameter space, $A$ is infinitely differentiable and
$$
\nabla A(\eta) = \mathbb{E}_\eta[S(X)], \qquad \nabla^2 A(\eta) = \mathrm{Cov}_\eta(S(X)) \succeq 0 .
$$
Hence $A$ is convex, and the maximum-likelihood equation for a sample $x_1, \dots, x_n$ is the moment equation $\nabla A(\eta) = \frac1n \sum_i S(x_i)$.

::: proof
Differentiate $e^{A(\eta)} = \int h\, e^{\langle \eta, S\rangle}$ under the integral sign, which dominated convergence allows in the interior. The first derivative gives $\nabla A\, e^{A} = \int S\, h\, e^{\langle \eta, S\rangle}$, that is $\nabla A = \mathbb{E}_\eta[S]$.

Differentiating once more gives
$$
\nabla^2 A + \nabla A\, \nabla A^\top = \mathbb{E}_\eta[S S^\top],
$$
which is the covariance formula. The log-likelihood $\langle \eta, \sum_i S(x_i)\rangle - nA(\eta)$ is concave, and its gradient vanishes exactly at the moment equation. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Chapters 3 and 7 use this structure: when the complete data of a latent-variable model form an exponential family, the EM algorithm only manipulates the expected sufficient statistics.

### 0.4 Smooth and strongly convex functions

::: def
[Definition 0.8 — Smoothness and strong convexity]{.tag} A differentiable function $F : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ is $L$-smooth if its gradient is $L$-Lipschitz:
$$
\|\nabla F(x) - \nabla F(y)\| \le L \|x - y\| .
$$
It is $\mu$-strongly convex ($\mu > 0$) if, for all $x, y$,
$$
F(y) \ge F(x) + \langle \nabla F(x), y - x \rangle + \frac{\mu}{2} \|y - x\|^2 .
$$
The ratio $\kappa = L / \mu \ge 1$ is the condition number.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.9 — Three consequences]{.tag} Let $F$ be $L$-smooth and $\mu$-strongly convex, with minimiser $x^*$ and $F^* = F(x^*)$.

1.  Descent lemma:
    $$
    F(y) \le F(x) + \langle \nabla F(x), y - x\rangle + \frac{L}{2}\|y - x\|^2 .
    $$
2.  Strong monotonicity:
    $$
    \langle \nabla F(x) - \nabla F(y), x - y \rangle \ge \mu \|x - y\|^2 .
    $$
3.  Gradient descent with step $1/L$ converges linearly:
    $$
    F(x_t) - F^* \le \Big(1 - \frac{\mu}{L}\Big)^t \big(F(x_0) - F^*\big).
    $$

::: proof
(1) Write $F(y) - F(x) - \langle \nabla F(x), y - x\rangle$ as the integral of $\langle \nabla F(x + s(y-x)) - \nabla F(x), y - x\rangle$ over $s \in [0, 1]$, and bound the integrand by $Ls\|y - x\|^2$.

(2) Add the strong convexity inequality written at $(x, y)$ and at $(y, x)$.

(3) Apply (1) with $y = x - \nabla F(x)/L$: one step decreases $F$ by at least $\|\nabla F(x)\|^2 / (2L)$.

Minimising both sides of the strong convexity inequality over $y$ gives $F^* \ge F(x) - \|\nabla F(x)\|^2/(2\mu)$, that is $\|\nabla F(x)\|^2 \ge 2\mu (F(x) - F^*)$.

Combining the two bounds gives $F(x_{t+1}) - F^* \le (1 - \mu/L)(F(x_t) - F^*)$, and induction concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The stochastic version of this argument is Theorem 1.3; the deterministic theory is developed in [Convex Optimization and Applications in Machine Learning](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html).

### 0.5 Martingales

::: def
[Definition 0.10 — Martingales]{.tag} Let $(\mathcal F_n)$ be a filtration. An adapted integrable sequence $(M_n)$ is a martingale if $\mathbb{E}[M_n \mid \mathcal F_{n-1}] = M_{n-1}$, and a supermartingale if $\mathbb{E}[M_n \mid \mathcal F_{n-1}] \le M_{n-1}$.

A sequence $(\xi_n)$ of martingale increments satisfies $\mathbb{E}[\xi_n \mid \mathcal F_{n-1}] = 0$. Martingale increments are uncorrelated, so the variance of their sum is the sum of their variances.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 0.11 — Martingale convergence (Doob)]{.tag} A nonnegative supermartingale converges almost surely to a finite limit. A martingale bounded in $L^2$, that is with $\sup_n \mathbb{E}[M_n^2] < \infty$, converges almost surely and in $L^2$.

The proofs (upcrossing inequality) are in Williams (1991), chapters 11–12.
:::

:::: prop
[Corollary 0.12 — Summable noise]{.tag} Let $(\xi_n)$ be martingale increments with $\mathbb{E}[\xi_n^2 \mid \mathcal F_{n-1}] \le C$, and $(\gamma_n)$ deterministic with $\sum_n \gamma_n^2 < \infty$. Then the series $\sum_n \gamma_n \xi_n$ converges almost surely.

::: proof
The partial sums $M_n = \sum_{k \le n} \gamma_k \xi_k$ form a martingale. By orthogonality of the increments,
$$
\mathbb{E}[M_n^2] = \sum_{k \le n} \gamma_k^2\, \mathbb{E}[\xi_k^2] \le C \sum_k \gamma_k^2 < \infty .
$$
Theorem 0.11 concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

This is the probabilistic half of the step-size condition $\sum_n \gamma_n^2 < \infty$ in stochastic approximation (ch. 4.2).

::: recap
**Key takeaways — chapter 0**

-   Monte Carlo error is $\sigma_h / \sqrt n$ in every dimension, but $\sigma_h$ can grow exponentially with the dimension.
-   $\mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p) \ge 0$ by Jensen's inequality, with equality only when $q = p$.
-   In an exponential family, $\nabla A$ is the mean of the sufficient statistic, and maximum likelihood is a moment equation.
-   For $L$-smooth, $\mu$-strongly convex functions, gradient descent contracts by $1 - \mu/L$ per step.
-   Nonnegative supermartingales and $L^2$-bounded martingales converge almost surely; noise weighted by square-summable steps is summable.
:::

## 1. The stochastic gradient algorithm {#ch1}

Fitting a model means minimising a risk that is an expectation, or an average over $n$ data points with $n$ in the millions. One exact gradient then costs a full pass over the data. The stochastic gradient algorithm replaces it with an unbiased estimate computed from a single sample.

This chapter proves when that works and at what rate, and lists what goes wrong in practice. The general theory of such noisy iterations is ch. 4.

### 1.1 The algorithm

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Stochastic optimisation problem and gradient oracle]{.tag} Let $\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be closed and convex, and $Z$ a random variable. The problem is
$$
\min_{\theta \in \Theta} F(\theta), \qquad F(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\big[f(\theta, Z)\big].
$$
Empirical risk minimisation is the special case where $Z$ is uniform over the $n$ data points, so that $F = \frac1n \sum_i f_i$.

A stochastic gradient oracle returns, at step $t$, the vector $g_t = \nabla_\theta f(\theta_{t-1}, Z_t)$ with $Z_t$ a fresh independent copy of $Z$. With $\mathcal F_t = \sigma(Z_1, \dots, Z_t)$ it is unbiased:
$$
\mathbb{E}[g_t \mid \mathcal F_{t-1}] = \nabla F(\theta_{t-1}).
$$
:::

::: def
[Algorithm 1.2 — Projected stochastic gradient descent (SGD)]{.tag} Start from $\theta_0 \in \Theta$ and choose step sizes $\gamma_t > 0$. For $t = 1, 2, \dots$
$$
\theta_t = \Pi_\Theta\big(\theta_{t-1} - \gamma_t\, g_t\big),
$$
where $\Pi_\Theta$ is the Euclidean projection onto $\Theta$ (the identity when $\Theta = \mathbb{R}^d$).
:::

For least squares, $f(\theta, (x, y)) = \frac12 (y - x^\top \theta)^2$ and the update reads
$$
\theta_t = \theta_{t-1} - \gamma_t\, (x_t^\top \theta_{t-1} - y_t)\, x_t .
$$
This is the least-mean-squares rule of adaptive signal processing.

The economics are simple. With $n = 10^6$ points in dimension $d = 100$, a full gradient costs about $2 \times 10^8$ operations and one stochastic gradient about $200$. One step of gradient descent therefore buys a million steps of SGD.

### 1.2 Convergence for strongly convex objectives

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.3 — Rate 1/t in the strongly convex case]{.tag} Assume that $F$ is $\mu$-strongly convex on $\Theta$ with minimiser $\theta^* \in \Theta$, and that the oracle has bounded second moment:
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\|g_t\|^2 \mid \mathcal F_{t-1}\big] \le B^2 .
$$
With the step sizes $\gamma_t = 1/(\mu t)$, the iterates of Algorithm 1.2 satisfy, for every $t \ge 1$,
$$
\mathbb{E}\,\|\theta_t - \theta^*\|^2 \le \frac{B^2}{\mu^2\, t} .
$$

::: proof
Write $\delta_t = \mathbb{E}\|\theta_t - \theta^*\|^2$.

1.  The projection is 1-Lipschitz and fixes $\theta^*$, so
    $$
    \|\theta_t - \theta^*\| \le \|\theta_{t-1} - \gamma_t g_t - \theta^*\| .
    $$
2.  Expanding the square and conditioning on $\mathcal F_{t-1}$:
    $$
    \mathbb{E}\big[\|\theta_t - \theta^*\|^2 \mid \mathcal F_{t-1}\big] \le \|\theta_{t-1} - \theta^*\|^2 - 2\gamma_t \langle \nabla F(\theta_{t-1}), \theta_{t-1} - \theta^* \rangle + \gamma_t^2 B^2 .
    $$
3.  Optimality of $\theta^*$ on $\Theta$ means that $\nabla F(\theta^*)$ makes a non-negative inner product with every $\theta - \theta^*$, $\theta \in \Theta$. Adding strong monotonicity (Proposition 0.9) yields
    $$
    \langle \nabla F(\theta), \theta - \theta^*\rangle \ge \mu \|\theta - \theta^*\|^2 .
    $$
4.  Taking expectations,
    $$
    \delta_t \le (1 - 2\mu\gamma_t)\, \delta_{t-1} + \gamma_t^2 B^2 .
    $$
5.  For $t = 1$ the factor is $1 - 2 = -1 \le 0$, so $\delta_1 \le B^2/\mu^2$.
6.  For $t \ge 2$, assume $\delta_{t-1} \le B^2 / (\mu^2 (t-1))$. Then
    $$
    \delta_t \le \frac{B^2}{\mu^2} \Big[\frac{t-2}{t(t-1)} + \frac{1}{t^2}\Big] \le \frac{B^2}{\mu^2 t},
    $$
    because $\frac{t-2}{t-1} + \frac1t \le 1$ is equivalent to $\frac1t \le \frac{1}{t-1}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

A gradient bound $B$ is incompatible with strong convexity on all of $\mathbb{R}^d$, since the gradient grows linearly. This is why the theorem is stated on a bounded convex set $\Theta$ with a projection. Corollary 4.5 removes this restriction for almost-sure convergence.
::::

::: note
[Remark 1.4 — The step size must know μ]{.tag} Take $\gamma_t = c/t$ instead. If $2\mu c < 1$, the rate degrades to $t^{-2\mu c}$, which can be arbitrarily slow.

Even without noise, on $F(\theta) = \mu\theta^2/2$ the iterates are $\theta_t = \theta_0 \prod_{s \le t}(1 - \mu c/s)$, of order $t^{-\mu c}$ (Exercise 7). Underestimating the curvature $\mu$ is harmless; overestimating it is not. Nemirovski, Juditsky, Lan and Shapiro (2009) made this point and advocated averaging (ch. 1.3 and Theorem 4.9).
:::

### 1.3 Convex objectives and averaging

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.5 — Rate 1/√T for the averaged iterate]{.tag} Assume that $F$ is convex with a minimiser $\theta^*$, that $\|\theta_0 - \theta^*\| \le D$, and that $\mathbb{E}[\|g_t\|^2 \mid \mathcal F_{t-1}] \le B^2$. Run $T$ steps with the constant step $\gamma = D / (B\sqrt T)$, and set
$$
\bar\theta_T = \frac1T \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} \theta_t .
$$
Then
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[F(\bar\theta_T)\big] - F(\theta^*) \le \frac{DB}{\sqrt T} .
$$

::: proof
1.  Steps 1–2 of the previous proof hold unchanged.
2.  Convexity bounds the gap $F(\theta) - F(\theta^*)$ by the inner product $\langle \nabla F(\theta), \theta - \theta^*\rangle$. Rearranging step 2 and taking expectations:
    $$
    \mathbb{E}\big[F(\theta_{t-1})\big] - F(\theta^*) \le \frac{\delta_{t-1} - \delta_t}{2\gamma} + \frac{\gamma B^2}{2} .
    $$
3.  Summing over $t = 1, \dots, T$, the first term telescopes and is at most $\delta_0 / (2\gamma) \le D^2/(2\gamma)$.
4.  Dividing by $T$ and using Jensen's inequality $F(\bar\theta_T) \le \frac1T\sum_t F(\theta_t)$:
    $$
    \mathbb{E}\big[F(\bar\theta_T)\big] - F(\theta^*) \le \frac{D^2}{2\gamma T} + \frac{\gamma B^2}{2} .
    $$
5.  The chosen $\gamma$ balances the two terms, each equal to $DB/(2\sqrt T)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

For non-smooth convex problems with a stochastic oracle, no algorithm can do better than order $DB/\sqrt T$ in the worst case (Nemirovski and Yudin, 1983). For smooth strongly convex problems, averaging with slowly decreasing steps reaches the optimal asymptotic variance without knowing $\mu$ (Theorem 4.9).
::::

### 1.4 Numerical bottlenecks

The theorems hide constants that dominate practice. Each bottleneck below has a precise source.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.6 — Constant step: fast forgetting, variance floor]{.tag} Under the assumptions of Theorem 1.3, with a constant step $\gamma \le 1/(2\mu)$,
$$
\mathbb{E}\,\|\theta_t - \theta^*\|^2 \le (1 - 2\mu\gamma)^t\, \|\theta_0 - \theta^*\|^2 + \frac{\gamma B^2}{2\mu} .
$$

::: proof
Unroll the recursion of step 4 of Theorem 1.3, $\delta_t \le (1 - 2\mu\gamma)\delta_{t-1} + \gamma^2 B^2$. The noise terms add up to at most
$$
\gamma^2 B^2 \sum_{k \ge 0} (1 - 2\mu\gamma)^k = \frac{\gamma B^2}{2\mu} .
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::

The initial error is forgotten geometrically, but the iterates then fluctuate at a level proportional to $\gamma$. Decreasing steps remove the floor at the price of a slower start.
::::

-   **Step size.** For least squares, a step larger than $2/\|x_t\|^2$ amplifies the error along $x_t$; a few such steps can make the iterates explode before $1/t$ steps become small. Practical schedules use $\gamma_t = \gamma_0 / (1 + \gamma_0 \mu t)$, which caps the first steps.
-   **Conditioning.** For least squares, the error along an eigenvector of the Hessian with eigenvalue $\lambda_j$ contracts like $(1 - \gamma\lambda_j)^t$. Directions with small $\lambda_j$ are slow; standardising the features and preconditioning reduce $\kappa = L/\mu$.
-   **Mini-batches.** Averaging $b$ stochastic gradients divides their variance by $b$ and multiplies the cost by $b$. This pays only when the $b$ gradients are computed in parallel.
-   **Finite sums.** For $F = \frac1n \sum_i f_i$, variance-reduced methods such as SVRG (Johnson and Zhang, 2013) and SAGA (Defazio, Bach and Lacoste-Julien, 2014) store or periodically recompute full gradients. They recover a linear rate for smooth strongly convex problems.
-   **Monitoring and non-convexity.** $F$ itself is too expensive to evaluate, so one tracks a running average of the sampled losses or a held-out loss. Without convexity, SGD only reaches approximate stationary points (Ghadimi and Lan, 2013).

::: ex
[Example 1.7 — Four step-size schedules on a least-squares stream]{.tag} Inputs $x \sim \mathcal N(0, H)$ in dimension $d = 10$, with the eigenvalues of $H$ spread from $\mu = 0.1$ to $L = 1$, and outputs $y = x^\top\theta^* + \varepsilon$ with unit noise.

The excess risk is
$$
F(\theta) - F(\theta^*) = \tfrac12 (\theta - \theta^*)^\top H\, (\theta - \theta^*).
$$
After $T$ samples, no estimator can beat about $\sigma^2 d / (2T)$.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
d, T = 10, 50_000
eig = np.linspace(0.1, 1.0, d)            # Hessian spectrum: mu = 0.1, L = 1
theta_star = np.ones(d)
X = np.sqrt(eig) * rng.standard_normal((T, d))
Y = X @ theta_star + rng.standard_normal(T)   # noise variance sigma^2 = 1

def excess_risk(theta):                    # F(theta) - F(theta*)
    return 0.5 * np.sum(eig * (theta - theta_star) ** 2)

def sgd(step, average=False):
    theta, avg = np.zeros(d), np.zeros(d)
    for t in range(1, T + 1):
        x, y = X[t - 1], Y[t - 1]
        theta = theta - step(t) * (x @ theta - y) * x    # stochastic gradient step
        avg += (theta - avg) / t                          # running Polyak-Ruppert average
    return excess_risk(avg if average else theta)

mu, L = 0.1, 1.0
runs = {
    "constant step 0.05": (lambda t: 0.05, False),
    "1/(mu (t + 2L/mu))": (lambda t: 1 / (mu * (t + 2 * L / mu)), False),
    "c/t with 2 mu c = 0.2": (lambda t: 1.0 / (t + 2), False),
    "0.5/sqrt(t), averaged": (lambda t: 0.5 / np.sqrt(t), True),
}
for name, (step, avg) in runs.items():
    print(f"{name:24s} excess risk = {sgd(step, avg):.2e}")
print(f"{'statistical limit':24s} sigma^2 d / (2T) = {d / (2 * T):.2e}")
```

The run prints excess risks of about $2 \times 10^{-1}$ for the constant step (the variance floor of Proposition 1.6), $2.5 \times 10^{-4}$ for the tuned $1/(\mu t)$ schedule, and $1.5 \times 10^{-2}$ for $c/t$ with $2\mu c = 0.2$ (Remark 1.4).

The averaged iterate with steps $0.5/\sqrt t$ reaches
$$
7.0 \times 10^{-5} \quad \text{against the limit } 1.0 \times 10^{-4},
$$
without knowing $\mu$: it is statistically optimal up to fluctuations.
:::

::: recap
**Key takeaways — chapter 1**

-   SGD uses unbiased gradients from single samples; one iteration costs $O(d)$ instead of $O(nd)$.
-   Strongly convex case: steps $1/(\mu t)$ give $\mathbb{E}\|\theta_t - \theta^*\|^2 \le B^2/(\mu^2 t)$, but $c/t$ with $2\mu c < 1$ is arbitrarily slow.
-   Convex case: the averaged iterate reaches $DB/\sqrt T$, which is optimal.
-   A constant step forgets the initialisation geometrically and then stalls at a floor proportional to $\gamma$.
-   Conditioning, step tuning and variance are the practical bottlenecks; averaging, preconditioning, mini-batches and variance reduction address them.
:::

## 2. Bayesian inference and its computational challenges {#ch2}

Bayesian inference treats the parameter as a random variable and conditions on the data. Every Bayesian answer — an estimator, a credible interval, a prediction, a model comparison — is then an integral against the posterior distribution.

This chapter introduces the framework briefly, then pinpoints which integrals are hard. Each obstacle it identifies is removed by one of the later chapters.

### 2.1 Prior, likelihood and posterior

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Bayesian model and posterior]{.tag} A Bayesian model is a statistical model $\{p(y \mid \theta) : \theta \in \Theta\}$ together with a prior density $\pi(\theta)$ on $\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$. Given data $y$, Bayes' formula defines the posterior density
$$
\pi(\theta \mid y) = \frac{p(y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta)}{p(y)}, \qquad p(y) = \int_\Theta p(y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta)\, d\theta .
$$
The normalising constant $p(y)$ is the evidence, or marginal likelihood. The posterior predictive density of a new observation is
$$
p(y_{\mathrm{new}} \mid y) = \int_\Theta p(y_{\mathrm{new}} \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta .
$$
:::

The posterior is known up to the constant $p(y)$ as soon as the likelihood and the prior can be evaluated. Much of the course is about doing statistics with a density known only up to a constant.

### 2.2 Bayes estimators

::: def
[Definition 2.2 — Bayes estimator]{.tag} Let $\ell(\theta, a) \ge 0$ be a loss measuring the cost of the decision $a$ when the parameter is $\theta$. The Bayes estimator minimises the posterior expected loss:
$$
\hat a(y) \in \arg\min_a\ \mathbb{E}\big[\ell(\theta, a) \mid y\big] .
$$
A credible region of level $1 - \alpha$ is a set $C(y)$ with posterior probability $1 - \alpha$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.3 — Three losses, three estimators]{.tag}

1.  The quadratic loss $\|\theta - a\|^2$ gives the posterior mean $\mathbb{E}[\theta \mid y]$.
2.  In dimension one, the absolute loss $|\theta - a|$ gives a posterior median.
3.  The loss $\mathbf 1\{\|\theta - a\| > \varepsilon\}$ gives, as $\varepsilon \to 0$ and for a continuous unimodal posterior, the posterior mode, also called the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimator.

::: proof
(1) With $m = \mathbb{E}[\theta \mid y]$, the cross term has zero posterior mean, so
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\|\theta - a\|^2 \mid y\big] = \mathbb{E}\big[\|\theta - m\|^2 \mid y\big] + \|m - a\|^2 ,
$$
which is minimal at $a = m$.

(2) The function $a \mapsto \mathbb{E}[|\theta - a| \mid y]$ is convex. Its right derivative is $P(\theta \le a \mid y) - P(\theta > a \mid y)$, which changes sign at a median.

(3) The expected loss is $1 - P(\|\theta - a\| \le \varepsilon \mid y)$. For small $\varepsilon$ it is close to $1 - \mathrm{vol}(B_\varepsilon)\, \pi(a \mid y)$, which is minimal where the posterior density is maximal. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 2.4 — Beta–Binomial conjugacy, by hand]{.tag} Observe $k$ successes in $n$ Bernoulli trials with success probability $\theta$, and take the prior $\mathrm{Beta}(a, b)$.

-   The posterior is proportional to the product of the likelihood and the prior,
    $$
    \theta^{k}(1-\theta)^{n-k} \cdot \theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1} ,
    $$
    so it is $\mathrm{Beta}(a + k,\, b + n - k)$. Prior and posterior belong to the same family: this is called conjugacy.
-   With $a = b = 2$, $n = 10$ and $k = 7$, the posterior is $\mathrm{Beta}(9, 5)$.
-   Its mean is $9/14 = 0.643$, its mode (MAP) is $8/12 = 0.667$, while the maximum-likelihood estimate is $0.7$.
-   The posterior mean is a weighted average of the prior mean $1/2$ (weight $4/14$) and of the empirical frequency $0.7$ (weight $10/14$): the prior acts like four extra observations.
:::

::: ex
[Example 2.5 — Posterior summaries and the evidence, numerically]{.tag} The evidence of Example 2.4 has a closed form,
$$
p(y) = \binom{n}{k} \frac{B(a + k,\, b + n - k)}{B(a, b)} = 120 \times \frac{6}{6435} = 0.11189 .
$$
The code compares it with adaptive quadrature and with the Laplace approximation of Proposition 2.7.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats, special, integrate

a, b, n, k = 2, 2, 10, 7                     # Beta(2, 2) prior, 7 successes out of 10
post = stats.beta(a + k, b + n - k)          # conjugacy: Beta(9, 5)
mode = (a + k - 1) / (a + b + n - 2)
print(f"posterior mean {post.mean():.4f}  median {post.median():.4f}  "
      f"MAP {mode:.4f}  MLE {k / n:.4f}")
print("95% credible interval", np.round(post.interval(0.95), 3))

# evidence p(y): closed form, adaptive quadrature, Laplace approximation
log_ev = np.log(special.comb(n, k)) + special.betaln(a + k, b + n - k) - special.betaln(a, b)
unnorm = lambda p: stats.binom.pmf(k, n, p) * stats.beta.pdf(p, a, b)
quad, _ = integrate.quad(unnorm, 0, 1)
f = lambda p: np.log(unnorm(p))
h = 1e-4
curv = -(f(mode + h) - 2 * f(mode) + f(mode - h)) / h ** 2   # -(log density)'' at the mode
laplace = unnorm(mode) * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi / curv)
print(f"evidence: exact {np.exp(log_ev):.5f}  quadrature {quad:.5f}  Laplace {laplace:.5f}")
```

The run prints the median $0.650$ and the equal-tailed 95 % credible interval $[0.386, 0.861]$. Quadrature reproduces the evidence to five digits, because the parameter is one-dimensional.

The Laplace approximation gives $0.1183$, a relative error of 6 % with ten observations; that error shrinks like $1/n$.
:::

### 2.3 Large samples: Bernstein–von Mises and Laplace

::: thm
[Theorem 2.6 — Bernstein–von Mises (statement)]{.tag} Let $Y_1, \dots, Y_n$ be independent with density $p(\cdot \mid \theta_0)$ in a regular parametric model with non-singular Fisher information $I(\theta_0)$. Assume that the prior is continuous and positive at $\theta_0$, and that uniformly consistent tests exist.

Then, with $\hat\theta_n$ the maximum-likelihood estimator, in probability under $\theta_0$,
$$
\Big\| \Pi(\cdot \mid Y_{1:n}) - \mathcal N\big(\hat\theta_n,\ \tfrac1n I(\theta_0)^{-1}\big) \Big\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \longrightarrow 0 .
$$
A proof is in van der Vaart (1998), Theorem 10.1.
:::

The posterior forgets the prior and becomes Gaussian around the maximum-likelihood estimator. Credible sets then become asymptotic confidence sets, and the posterior mean, median and mode agree to first order.

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.7 — Laplace approximation of the evidence]{.tag} Let $\hat\theta$ be the posterior mode and $H$ the Hessian of $-\log\big(p(y \mid \theta)\pi(\theta)\big)$ at $\hat\theta$, assumed positive definite. Then
$$
p(y) \approx p(y \mid \hat\theta)\, \pi(\hat\theta)\, (2\pi)^{d/2} \det(H)^{-1/2} .
$$
For $n$ independent observations the relative error is $O(1/n)$ under smoothness assumptions.

::: proof
*Sketch.* Expand $\log(p(y \mid \theta)\pi(\theta))$ to second order at $\hat\theta$. The gradient vanishes, and the quadratic term is the negative quadratic form of $H$ applied to $\theta - \hat\theta$, divided by 2.

Integrating the resulting Gaussian function gives the formula. The Hessian grows linearly with $n$, so the posterior mass concentrates in a region of radius $n^{-1/2}$ where the cubic remainder is $O(n^{-1/2})$. Its odd part integrates to zero, which leaves a relative error of order $1/n$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

These asymptotics fail exactly where computational statistics is needed: small samples, multimodal posteriors, parameters on a boundary, and latent-variable models whose number of hidden variables grows with $n$.

### 2.4 Where the computations get hard

::: key
[Key formula — every Bayesian answer is a ratio of integrals]{.tag}
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[h(\theta) \mid y\big] = \frac{\int_\Theta h(\theta)\, p(y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta)\, d\theta}{\int_\Theta p(y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta)\, d\theta}
$$
:::

Four obstacles make this ratio hard to compute, and each is removed by a later chapter.

1.  **Dimension.** A grid with $m$ points per axis needs $m^d$ evaluations: $10^{20}$ for $m = 10$ and $d = 20$. Monte Carlo (ch. 0.1) avoids the grid but needs samples from the posterior, which is known only up to $p(y)$. Rejection and importance sampling (ch. 5) work in small dimension; MCMC (ch. 6) works in general; adaptive MCMC and tempering (ch. 8) make it robust.
2.  **Hidden variables.** In many models the likelihood is itself an integral over unobserved variables. Even the maximum-likelihood or MAP estimator then requires EM (ch. 3), and stochastic versions of EM when the E-step is an intractable integral (ch. 7).
3.  **No likelihood at all.** Simulators in population genetics or epidemiology can generate data but cannot evaluate $p(y \mid \theta)$. Approximate Bayesian computation (ch. 9) works with simulations only.
4.  **Large data.** When each evaluation of the likelihood costs $n$ operations, stochastic gradients (ch. 1) and stochastic approximation (ch. 4) replace full passes over the data by single samples.

The constant $p(y)$ cancels in the ratio $\pi(\theta' \mid y)/\pi(\theta \mid y)$. This simple remark is what makes the Metropolis–Hastings algorithm (ch. 6.2) possible.

### 2.5 Latent-variable models

::: def
[Definition 2.8 — Latent-variable (incomplete-data) model]{.tag} The complete data are a pair $(y, z)$ with density $p(y, z; \theta)$, of which only $y$ is observed. The likelihood of the observed data is
$$
p(y; \theta) = \int p(y, z; \theta)\, dz ,
$$
and the conditional density of the hidden variables, $p(z \mid y; \theta) = p(y, z; \theta)/p(y; \theta)$, plays the role of a posterior.
:::

::: ex
[Example 2.9 — Three latent-variable models of the course]{.tag}

-   **Gaussian mixture.** $z_i \in \{1, \dots, K\}$ with $P(z_i = k) = w_k$, and $y_i \mid z_i = k \sim \mathcal N(\mu_k, \sigma_k^2)$. The integral is a finite sum, but the log-likelihood is a sum of logarithms of sums, with no closed-form maximiser (ch. 3.4).
-   **Mixed-effects model.** Subject $i$ has a random parameter $\varphi_i \sim \mathcal N(\mu, \Omega)$, and $y_{ij} = g(t_{ij}, \varphi_i) + \sigma \varepsilon_{ij}$. When $g$ is nonlinear, as in pharmacokinetics or growth curves, the integral over $\varphi_i$ has no closed form (ch. 7).
-   **Random-effects logistic regression.** Given $\varphi_i \sim \mathcal N(\mu, \omega^2)$, the answers $y_{ij}$ are Bernoulli with success probability $\sigma(\varphi_i)$, where $\sigma$ is the logistic function. This is the running example of ch. 7.
:::

A Bayesian model is itself a latent-variable model in which $\theta$ is the hidden variable. This is why the same simulation tools serve both for computing posteriors and for maximising likelihoods with hidden variables.

::: recap
**Key takeaways — chapter 2**

-   Posterior $\propto$ likelihood $\times$ prior; the normalising constant $p(y)$ is an integral, usually unknown.
-   Quadratic, absolute and 0–1 losses give the posterior mean, median and mode.
-   With many observations the posterior is approximately Gaussian (Bernstein–von Mises), and the Laplace approximation estimates $p(y)$ with relative error $O(1/n)$.
-   The obstacles are dimension, hidden variables, intractable likelihoods and data size; they motivate MCMC, EM, ABC and stochastic gradients respectively.
-   Latent-variable models have likelihoods defined by integrals over hidden variables.
:::

## 3. Majorize–Minimize and the EM algorithm {#ch3}

When the likelihood is an integral over hidden variables, direct maximisation is awkward, while the complete-data likelihood is often simple. The EM algorithm exploits this: at each step it maximises a surrogate that touches the log-likelihood from below.

Seen from further away, EM is one instance of a general principle, Majorize–Minimize, which we state first.

### 3.1 The Majorize–Minimize principle

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Majorizing surrogate and MM algorithm]{.tag} A function $g(\cdot \mid \theta')$ majorizes $F$ at $\theta'$ if
$$
g(\theta \mid \theta') \ge F(\theta) \ \text{ for all } \theta, \qquad g(\theta' \mid \theta') = F(\theta') .
$$
The Majorize–Minimize (MM) algorithm iterates
$$
\theta_{k+1} \in \arg\min_\theta\, g(\theta \mid \theta_k) .
$$
For a maximisation problem, one minorizes and maximises instead: this is the same algorithm applied to $-F$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.2 — Descent property]{.tag} Every MM iteration decreases the objective:
$$
F(\theta_{k+1}) \le F(\theta_k) .
$$

::: proof
The chain
$$
F(\theta_{k+1}) \le g(\theta_{k+1} \mid \theta_k) \le g(\theta_k \mid \theta_k) = F(\theta_k)
$$
uses the majorization, then the minimisation step, then the tangency. [∎]{.qed}
:::

The proof only uses the decrease of the surrogate from $\theta_k$ to $\theta_{k+1}$. Any decrease of the surrogate, not necessarily its minimum, keeps the descent property.
::::

::: ex
[Example 3.3 — Two classical surrogates]{.tag}

-   **Quadratic surrogate.** If $F$ is $L$-smooth, the descent lemma (Proposition 0.9) gives the majorizer
    $$
    g(\theta \mid \theta') = F(\theta') + \langle \nabla F(\theta'), \theta - \theta'\rangle + \frac{L}{2}\|\theta - \theta'\|^2 .
    $$
    Its minimiser is $\theta' - \nabla F(\theta')/L$: gradient descent with step $1/L$ is an MM algorithm.
-   **Absolute value.** For $r' \ne 0$, the inequality $(|r| - |r'|)^2 \ge 0$ gives
    $$
    |r| \le \frac{r^2}{2|r'|} + \frac{|r'|}{2} ,
    $$
    with equality at $r = \pm r'$. For least absolute deviations, the surrogate is a weighted least-squares problem with weights $1/|r_i(\theta_k)|$: iteratively reweighted least squares (Exercise 8).
:::

Lange, Hunter and Yang (2000) and Hunter and Lange (2004) survey MM algorithms. Mairal (2015) extends them to large finite sums with incremental surrogates.

### 3.2 EM as a minorize–maximize algorithm

Consider a latent-variable model (Definition 2.8) and the log-likelihood $\ell(\theta) = \log p(y; \theta)$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.4 — Evidence lower bound]{.tag} For every $\theta$ and every density $q$ on the hidden variables,
$$
\ell(\theta) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_q\big[\log p(y, Z; \theta) - \log q(Z)\big]}_{\mathcal L(q,\, \theta)} + \mathrm{KL}\big(q \,\|\, p(\cdot \mid y; \theta)\big) .
$$
Consequently $\mathcal L(q, \theta) \le \ell(\theta)$, with equality if and only if $q = p(\cdot \mid y; \theta)$.

::: proof
For every $z$, Bayes' formula gives
$$
\log p(y; \theta) = \log p(y, z; \theta) - \log p(z \mid y; \theta) .
$$
Add and subtract $\log q(z)$, then integrate against $q$. The inequality and its equality case follow from Gibbs' inequality (Proposition 0.5). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Algorithm 3.5 — Expectation–Maximisation (Dempster, Laird and Rubin, 1977)]{.tag} Start from $\theta_0$. For $k = 0, 1, \dots$

-   **E-step:** compute the expected complete-data log-likelihood
    $$
    Q(\theta \mid \theta_k) = \mathbb{E}_{\theta_k}\big[\log p(y, Z; \theta) \mid y\big] .
    $$
-   **M-step:** set
    $$
    \theta_{k+1} \in \arg\max_\theta\, Q(\theta \mid \theta_k) .
    $$
:::

With $q_k = p(\cdot \mid y; \theta_k)$, the lower bound $\mathcal L(q_k, \theta)$ equals $Q(\theta \mid \theta_k)$ plus a term that does not depend on $\theta$.

EM therefore maximises, at each step, a minorizer of $\ell$ that touches it at $\theta_k$: it is an MM algorithm for $-\ell$.

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.6 — EM increases the likelihood]{.tag} Every EM iteration satisfies
$$
\ell(\theta_{k+1}) \ge \ell(\theta_k) .
$$

::: proof
With $q_k = p(\cdot \mid y; \theta_k)$, Proposition 3.4 and the M-step give
$$
\ell(\theta_{k+1}) \ge \mathcal L(q_k, \theta_{k+1}) \ge \mathcal L(q_k, \theta_k) = \ell(\theta_k) .
$$
The first inequality is the lower bound, the second is the M-step, and the equality is the case $q = p(\cdot \mid y; \theta_k)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Neal and Hinton (1998) read EM as coordinate ascent on $\mathcal L(q, \theta)$: the E-step maximises over $q$, the M-step over $\theta$. This view justifies partial E-steps, incremental variants and variational EM, where $q$ is restricted to a tractable family.

### 3.3 Exponential-family complete data

Assume that the complete data form a curved exponential family (Definition 0.6),
$$
p(y, z; \theta) = h(y, z) \exp\big(\langle \varphi(\theta), S(y, z) \rangle - \psi(\theta)\big),
$$
with $\varphi : \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}^q$. Then, up to a constant,
$$
Q(\theta \mid \theta_k) = \langle \varphi(\theta), s_k \rangle - \psi(\theta),
$$
where $s_k$ is the conditional expectation of $S(y, Z)$ under $\theta_k$.

::: def
[Algorithm 3.7 — EM in sufficient statistics]{.tag} Define the expected statistic and the M-step map
$$
\bar s(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_\theta\big[S(y, Z) \mid y\big], \qquad \bar\theta(s) = \arg\max_\theta\ \big\{\langle \varphi(\theta), s\rangle - \psi(\theta)\big\} .
$$
EM is the fixed-point iteration $s_{k+1} = \bar s(\bar\theta(s_k))$, with $\theta_k = \bar\theta(s_k)$.
:::

The E-step is an expectation of a fixed function; the M-step is usually explicit, as for complete-data maximum likelihood. Stochastic versions of EM (ch. 7) keep the M-step and replace the expectation $\bar s$ by simulation.

### 3.4 Gaussian mixtures

::: ex
[Example 3.8 — EM for a Gaussian mixture]{.tag} For $K$ one-dimensional components with weights $w_k$, means $\mu_k$ and variances $\sigma_k^2$:

-   **E-step:** the responsibilities are the posterior probabilities of the labels,
    $$
    r_{ik} = \frac{w_k\, \mathcal N(y_i; \mu_k, \sigma_k^2)}{\sum_j w_j\, \mathcal N(y_i; \mu_j, \sigma_j^2)} .
    $$
-   **M-step:** with $n_k = \sum_i r_{ik}$,
    $$
    w_k = \frac{n_k}{n}, \qquad \mu_k = \frac{1}{n_k}\sum_i r_{ik}\, y_i, \qquad \sigma_k^2 = \frac{1}{n_k}\sum_i r_{ik} (y_i - \mu_k)^2 .
    $$
-   **Derivation:** up to a constant,
    $$
    Q = \sum_{i,k} r_{ik}\big[\log w_k + \log \mathcal N(y_i; \mu_k, \sigma_k^2)\big] .
    $$
    A Lagrange multiplier for $\sum_k w_k = 1$ gives $w_k \propto n_k$, and the Gaussian terms are weighted maximum-likelihood problems.

The code fits two components to $n = 1000$ points drawn with weights $(0.3, 0.7)$, means $(3, 0)$ and unit variances, and checks the monotonicity of Theorem 3.6.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n = 1000
z = rng.random(n) < 0.3                                   # hidden labels, P(z = 1) = 0.3
y = np.where(z, rng.normal(3.0, 1.0, n), rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, n))

def loglik(w, m, s):
    return np.log(w * norm.pdf(y, m[0], s[0]) + (1 - w) * norm.pdf(y, m[1], s[1])).sum()

w, m, s = 0.5, np.array([1.0, -1.0]), np.array([2.0, 2.0])  # w = weight of component 0
trace = [loglik(w, m, s)]
for it in range(200):
    p0 = w * norm.pdf(y, m[0], s[0])
    p1 = (1 - w) * norm.pdf(y, m[1], s[1])
    r = p0 / (p0 + p1)                                     # E-step: responsibilities
    w = r.mean()                                           # M-step: weighted moments
    m = np.array([r @ y / r.sum(), (1 - r) @ y / (1 - r).sum()])
    s = np.sqrt(np.array([r @ (y - m[0]) ** 2 / r.sum(),
                          (1 - r) @ (y - m[1]) ** 2 / (1 - r).sum()]))
    trace.append(loglik(w, m, s))

trace = np.array(trace)
print("log-likelihood at iterations 0, 1, 5, 20, 200:", np.round(trace[[0, 1, 5, 20, 200]], 2))
print("monotone:", bool(np.all(np.diff(trace) > -1e-9)))
print(f"weights ({w:.3f}, {1 - w:.3f})  means {np.round(m, 3)}  std {np.round(s, 3)}")
```

The log-likelihood goes through $-2109.1$, $-1956.1$, $-1923.5$, $-1913.8$ and $-1900.7$, and never decreases. It still gains 13 units between iterations 20 and 200: the components overlap, so EM is slow (Proposition 3.10).

The final estimates are weights $(0.268, 0.732)$, means $(3.21, 0.06)$ and standard deviations $(0.94, 1.07)$.
:::

The likelihood of a Gaussian mixture is unbounded: centring one component on a data point and letting its variance tend to zero sends $\ell$ to $+\infty$. EM finds local maxima, not this degenerate supremum. In practice one bounds the variances from below or adds a prior and runs MAP-EM, which adds $\log \pi(\theta)$ to $Q$.

### 3.5 Convergence and speed

::: thm
[Theorem 3.9 — Limit points of EM (Wu, 1983; statement)]{.tag} Assume that $\ell$ is continuous, that the level set $\{\theta : \ell(\theta) \ge \ell(\theta_0)\}$ is compact, and that $Q(\theta \mid \theta')$ is continuous in both arguments and differentiable in $\theta$.

Then $\ell(\theta_k)$ increases to a limit $\ell^*$, and every limit point of $(\theta_k)$ is a stationary point of $\ell$ with $\ell = \ell^*$. These may be local maxima or saddle points, not necessarily the global maximum.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.10 — Rate of EM: the fraction of missing information]{.tag} Let $\theta^*$ be a limit of EM, and write $M$ for the EM map $\theta_k \mapsto \theta_{k+1}$. Define the complete, missing and observed informations at $\theta^*$:
$$
I_c = -\mathbb{E}\big[\nabla^2 \log p(y, Z; \theta) \mid y\big], \quad I_m = -\mathbb{E}\big[\nabla^2 \log p(Z \mid y; \theta) \mid y\big], \quad I_{\mathrm{obs}} = -\nabla^2 \ell(\theta^*) ,
$$
so that $I_{\mathrm{obs}} = I_c - I_m$. If $I_c$ is invertible, then
$$
DM(\theta^*) = I_c^{-1} I_m = \mathrm{Id} - I_c^{-1} I_{\mathrm{obs}} .
$$

::: proof
1.  The M-step gives $\nabla_\theta Q(M(\theta') \mid \theta') = 0$ for all $\theta'$. Differentiate in $\theta'$ at $\theta^*$, a fixed point:
    $$
    \nabla^2_{\theta\theta} Q\, DM(\theta^*) + \nabla^2_{\theta\theta'} Q = 0 .
    $$
2.  By definition, the Hessian of $Q(\cdot \mid \theta^*)$ at $\theta^*$ is $-I_c$.
3.  The complete log-likelihood is $\ell(\theta) + \log p(z \mid y; \theta)$ and $\nabla \ell(\theta^*) = 0$. Hence the cross derivative is the conditional covariance of the score $\nabla \log p(Z \mid y; \theta^*)$. By the information identity, this covariance equals $I_m$.
4.  Hence $-I_c\, DM + I_m = 0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Near $\theta^*$, EM converges linearly with rate the spectral radius of $I_c^{-1} I_m$, the largest fraction of missing information. Well-separated mixture components give fast convergence, and overlapping ones a rate close to 1, as in Example 3.8.
::::

::: note
[Variants]{.tag} Generalised EM only increases $Q$ in the M-step, and ECM (Meng and Rubin, 1993) does it by conditional maximisations. Accelerations such as SQUAREM (Varadhan and Roland, 2008) extrapolate the EM map.

Louis (1982) computes the observed information $I_{\mathrm{obs}} = I_c - I_m$ from EM quantities, which gives standard errors. Online EM (Cappé and Moulines, 2009) processes data streams with a stochastic approximation of $\bar s$, the idea of ch. 7.
:::

::: recap
**Key takeaways — chapter 3**

-   MM minimises a surrogate that majorizes the objective and touches it at the current point; the objective decreases at every step.
-   The log-likelihood is the lower bound $\mathcal L(q, \theta)$ plus a KL gap: EM alternates exact maximisation over $q$ (E-step) and over $\theta$ (M-step).
-   EM never decreases the likelihood, and its limit points are stationary points (Wu, 1983).
-   In exponential families EM iterates $s \mapsto \bar s(\bar\theta(s))$ on expected sufficient statistics.
-   EM converges linearly at a rate equal to the largest fraction of missing information, $I_c^{-1} I_m$.
:::

## 4. Stochastic approximation {#ch4}

SGD (ch. 1), the stochastic versions of EM (ch. 7) and adaptive MCMC (ch. 8) share one structure: a parameter moves along a noisy estimate of a mean field, with decreasing steps. Stochastic approximation, started by Robbins and Monro in 1951, studies this structure once and for all.

This chapter gives the convergence conditions that the syllabus asks for, with a complete proof in the Lyapunov case, then the rates and the effect of averaging.

### 4.1 The Robbins–Monro algorithm

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Robbins–Monro algorithm]{.tag} Let $H(\theta, x)$ be a function and $X$ a random variable such that the mean field
$$
h(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\big[H(\theta, X)\big]
$$
is defined for all $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^d$. The goal is a root $\theta^*$ of $h$, using only the values of $H$.

With independent copies $X_n$ of $X$ and steps $\gamma_n > 0$, the algorithm is
$$
\theta_n = \theta_{n-1} + \gamma_n H(\theta_{n-1}, X_n) = \theta_{n-1} + \gamma_n \big(h(\theta_{n-1}) + \xi_n\big),
$$
where $\xi_n = H(\theta_{n-1}, X_n) - h(\theta_{n-1})$ is a martingale increment for $\mathcal F_n = \sigma(X_1, \dots, X_n)$.
:::

::: ex
[Example 4.2 — Four instances]{.tag}

-   **Mean.** $H(\theta, x) = x - \theta$ with $\gamma_n = 1/n$ gives $\theta_n = \frac1n\sum_{k \le n} X_k$, the empirical mean.
-   **SGD.** $H(\theta, z) = -\nabla_\theta f(\theta, z)$ gives the mean field $h = -\nabla F$, whose roots are the critical points of $F$.
-   **Quantile.** $H(\theta, x) = \alpha - \mathbf 1\{x \le \theta\}$ gives $h(\theta) = \alpha - F_X(\theta)$, whose root is the $\alpha$-quantile of $X$. No density is ever evaluated.
-   **Later in the course.** SAEM (ch. 7) and adaptive Metropolis (ch. 8) update sufficient statistics and proposal covariances with exactly this recursion.
:::

### 4.2 Step-size conditions

::: key
[Key result — the Robbins–Monro step-size conditions]{.tag}
$$
\sum_{n \ge 1} \gamma_n = \infty, \qquad \sum_{n \ge 1} \gamma_n^2 < \infty
$$
:::

The first condition lets the iterates travel any distance: the deterministic part moves by $\sum_n \gamma_n h(\theta_{n-1})$. The second makes the accumulated noise $\sum_n \gamma_n \xi_n$ converge (Corollary 0.12). Steps $\gamma_n = \gamma_0 n^{-a}$ satisfy both when $1/2 < a \le 1$.

### 4.3 The Robbins–Siegmund lemma

:::: thm
[Lemma 4.3 — Robbins and Siegmund (1971)]{.tag} Let $(a_n)$ and $(b_n)$ be deterministic nonnegative sequences with finite sums, and $(V_n)$, $(c_n)$ nonnegative adapted sequences with $c_n$ measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_{n-1}$. Assume that
$$
\mathbb{E}[V_n \mid \mathcal F_{n-1}] \le (1 + a_n)\, V_{n-1} + b_n - c_n \quad \text{for all } n .
$$
Then $V_n$ converges almost surely to a finite limit, and $\sum_n c_n < \infty$ almost surely.

::: proof
1.  Let $\alpha_n = \prod_{k \le n} (1 + a_k)$. It increases to a finite limit $\alpha_\infty$ because $\sum a_k < \infty$, and $\alpha_n \ge 1$.
2.  Divide by $\alpha_n$: with $V'_n = V_n/\alpha_n$, $b'_n = b_n/\alpha_n$ and $c'_n = c_n/\alpha_n$,
    $$
    \mathbb{E}[V'_n \mid \mathcal F_{n-1}] \le V'_{n-1} + b'_n - c'_n .
    $$
3.  Set $U_n = V'_n + \sum_{k \le n} c'_k + \sum_{k > n} b'_k$. Step 2 gives $\mathbb{E}[U_n \mid \mathcal F_{n-1}] \le U_{n-1}$. Since $U_n \ge 0$, Theorem 0.11 shows that $U_n$ converges almost surely to a finite limit.
4.  Because $V'_n \ge 0$, the partial sums $\sum_{k \le n} c'_k \le U_n$ are bounded, so $\sum_k c'_k < \infty$. Then $V'_n$ converges, as a difference of convergent sequences.
5.  Multiplying back by $\alpha_n \to \alpha_\infty$, $V_n$ converges, and $\sum_k c_k \le \alpha_\infty \sum_k c'_k < \infty$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 4.4 Almost-sure convergence

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.4 — Convergence of Robbins–Monro, Lyapunov form]{.tag} Let $\theta^*$ be a root of $h$ and $c(\theta) = -\langle \theta - \theta^*, h(\theta) \rangle$. Assume:

1.  $c(\theta) \ge 0$ for all $\theta$, and $c$ is bounded below by a positive constant on every annulus $\varepsilon \le \|\theta - \theta^*\| \le 1/\varepsilon$, $0 < \varepsilon < 1$;
2.  the growth condition holds: for all $\theta$,
    $$
    \mathbb{E}\|H(\theta, X)\|^2 \le C\,(1 + \|\theta - \theta^*\|^2) ;
    $$
3.  the step-size conditions of ch. 4.2.

Then $\theta_n \to \theta^*$ almost surely.

::: proof
1.  Let $V_n = \|\theta_n - \theta^*\|^2$. Expanding the recursion,
    $$
    V_n = V_{n-1} + 2\gamma_n \langle \theta_{n-1} - \theta^*, H(\theta_{n-1}, X_n) \rangle + \gamma_n^2 \|H(\theta_{n-1}, X_n)\|^2 .
    $$
2.  Conditioning on $\mathcal F_{n-1}$ and using assumption 2:
    $$
    \mathbb{E}[V_n \mid \mathcal F_{n-1}] \le (1 + C\gamma_n^2)\, V_{n-1} + C\gamma_n^2 - 2\gamma_n\, c(\theta_{n-1}) .
    $$
3.  Lemma 4.3, applied with $a_n = b_n = C\gamma_n^2$, gives $V_n \to V_\infty$ almost surely, and the series $\sum_n \gamma_n c(\theta_{n-1})$ converges almost surely.
4.  Suppose $V_\infty > 0$ on an event of positive probability. On that event, the convergent sequence $(\theta_n)$ eventually stays in an annulus $\varepsilon \le \|\theta - \theta^*\| \le 1/\varepsilon$, for some rational $\varepsilon$.
5.  There $c(\theta_{n-1}) \ge \eta > 0$ by assumption 1, so $\sum_n \gamma_n c(\theta_{n-1}) = \infty$ because $\sum_n \gamma_n = \infty$. This contradicts step 3, hence $V_\infty = 0$ almost surely. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Corollary 4.5 — Almost-sure convergence of SGD]{.tag} Let $F$ be $\mu$-strongly convex with minimiser $\theta^*$. Assume that the stochastic gradients satisfy the growth condition of Theorem 4.4. Then unprojected SGD with $\sum \gamma_n = \infty$ and $\sum \gamma_n^2 < \infty$ converges almost surely to $\theta^*$.

::: proof
Here $h = -\nabla F$, so Proposition 0.9 gives
$$
c(\theta) = \langle \nabla F(\theta), \theta - \theta^* \rangle \ge \mu \|\theta - \theta^*\|^2 .
$$ Assumption 1 holds, and Theorem 4.4 applies. [∎]{.qed}
:::

For least squares, the growth condition holds as soon as the inputs have a finite fourth moment and the noise a finite second moment. No bounded domain is needed, unlike Theorem 1.3.
::::

::: ex
[Example 4.6 — Quantile estimation satisfies the assumptions]{.tag} For $H(\theta, x) = \alpha - \mathbf 1\{x \le \theta\}$ with $F_X$ continuous and strictly increasing:

-   $c(\theta) = (\theta - \theta^*)(F_X(\theta) - \alpha)$ is positive for $\theta \ne \theta^*$ and bounded below on every annulus;
-   $|H| \le 1$, so the growth condition holds with $C = 1$.

Theorem 4.4 shows that the recursive quantile estimator converges almost surely, without ever sorting the data.
:::

### 4.5 The ODE method

When the mean field has several roots, as for non-convex SGD or for EM-like fixed points, no single quadratic Lyapunov function exists. The standard tool compares the iterates with the solutions of the ordinary differential equation $\dot\theta = h(\theta)$: the steps $\gamma_n$ play the role of time increments, and the noise averages out.

::: thm
[Theorem 4.7 — ODE method (statement)]{.tag} Assume:

1.  $h$ is continuous, and there is a $C^1$ function $V$ with $\langle \nabla V(\theta), h(\theta) \rangle \le 0$ for all $\theta$;
2.  the set $\mathcal L$ of points where $\langle \nabla V, h \rangle = 0$ is such that $V(\mathcal L)$ has empty interior;
3.  the sequence $(\theta_n)$ stays almost surely in a compact set;
4.  $\sum_n \gamma_n = \infty$ and the series $\sum_n \gamma_n \xi_n$ converges almost surely.

Then the distance from $\theta_n$ to $\mathcal L$ tends to 0 almost surely. See Kushner and Yin (2003), Benaïm (1999), and Delyon, Lavielle and Moulines (1999, Theorem 2) for the form used by SAEM.
:::

For SGD, $V = F$ and $\mathcal L$ is the set of critical points. For SAEM, $V$ is minus the log-likelihood read through the M-step map (Proposition 7.4).

Assumption 3, stability, is the delicate one in practice. A classical remedy is truncation on randomly varying bounds: the iterate is re-initialised whenever it leaves a compact set, and the compact set grows after each re-initialisation (Andrieu, Moulines and Priouret, 2005).

### 4.6 Rates and averaging

::: thm
[Theorem 4.8 — Central limit theorem (statement)]{.tag} Assume that $\theta_n \to \theta^*$ and that the Jacobian $A = Dh(\theta^*)$ has eigenvalues with negative real parts. Let $\Gamma$ be the limiting covariance of the noise $\xi_n$, and take $\gamma_n = \gamma_0 n^{-a}$.

-   If $1/2 < a < 1$, then $\gamma_n^{-1/2}(\theta_n - \theta^*)$ converges in law to $\mathcal N(0, \Sigma)$, where $A\Sigma + \Sigma A^\top + \Gamma = 0$.
-   If $a = 1$ and $\gamma_0 A + \mathrm{Id}/2$ also has eigenvalues with negative real parts, then $\sqrt n\,(\theta_n - \theta^*)$ converges in law to a centred Gaussian.

In dimension 1, with $h'(\theta^*) = -\lambda < 0$ and $a = 1$, the asymptotic variance is
$$
\frac{\gamma_0^2\, \Gamma}{2\gamma_0 \lambda - 1} \qquad (\gamma_0 \lambda > 1/2),
$$
minimal at $\gamma_0 = 1/\lambda$ where it equals $\Gamma/\lambda^2$. References: Benveniste, Métivier and Priouret (1990); Kushner and Yin (2003).
:::

The optimal step $1/(\lambda n)$ requires the unknown slope $\lambda$; when $\gamma_0\lambda < 1/2$ the error decays only like $n^{-\gamma_0\lambda}$, the phenomenon of Remark 1.4. Averaging removes this dependence.

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.9 — Polyak–Ruppert averaging (Polyak and Juditsky, 1992)]{.tag} Under the assumptions of Theorem 4.8 with $1/2 < a < 1$, the average $\bar\theta_n = \frac1n \sum_{k=1}^n \theta_k$ satisfies
$$
\sqrt n\, (\bar\theta_n - \theta^*) \xrightarrow{\ \mathcal L\ } \mathcal N\big(0,\ A^{-1}\Gamma A^{-\top}\big).
$$
This covariance is the smallest achievable by any such recursion, and it is reached without knowing $A$.

::: proof
*Sketch for a linear mean field* $h(\theta) = A(\theta - \theta^*)$.

1.  The recursion gives
    $$
    \theta_{k-1} - \theta^* = A^{-1}\Big[\frac{\theta_k - \theta_{k-1}}{\gamma_k} - \xi_k\Big] .
    $$
2.  Averaging over $k \le n$:
    $$
    \bar\theta_{n} - \theta^* \approx -A^{-1}\,\frac1n \sum_{k \le n} \xi_k + \frac{A^{-1}}{n} \sum_{k \le n} \frac{\theta_k - \theta_{k-1}}{\gamma_k} .
    $$
3.  An Abel summation shows that the second term is of order $1/(n\gamma_n)$ times the size of the iterates' error. This is $o(n^{-1/2})$ precisely when $a < 1$.
4.  The martingale central limit theorem applied to the first term gives the covariance $A^{-1}\Gamma A^{-\top}/n$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 4.10 — The 0.9-quantile of an exponential law]{.tag} For $X \sim \mathrm{Exp}(1)$ and $\alpha = 0.9$:

-   the target is $\theta^* = \log 10 = 2.3026$;
-   the slope is $h'(\theta^*) = -f_X(\theta^*) = -0.1$, so $\lambda = 0.1$;
-   the noise variance at $\theta^*$ is $\Gamma = \alpha(1 - \alpha) = 0.09$;
-   the optimal asymptotic variance is $\Gamma / \lambda^2 = 9$, the same as for the empirical quantile.

With $\gamma_n = 1/n$, $\gamma_0\lambda = 0.1 < 1/2$ and the error decays like $n^{-0.1}$ only. With $\gamma_n = 10/n$ the step is optimal. Averaging with $\gamma_n = n^{-2/3}$ needs no knowledge of $\lambda$.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
alpha, N = 0.9, 100_000
target = np.log(10.0)                      # 0.9-quantile of Exp(1); f(target) = 0.1
X = rng.exponential(size=N)

def robbins_monro(step, average=False):
    th, avg = 0.0, 0.0
    for n in range(1, N + 1):
        th += step(n) * (alpha - (X[n - 1] <= th))   # H(theta, X) = alpha - 1{X <= theta}
        avg += (th - avg) / n
    return avg if average else th

for name, step, av in [("gamma_n = 1/n", lambda n: 1.0 / n, False),
                       ("gamma_n = 10/n", lambda n: 10.0 / n, False),
                       ("n^(-2/3), averaged", lambda n: n ** (-2 / 3), True)]:
    print(f"{name:20s} error = {robbins_monro(step, av) - target:+.4f}")
```

After $N = 10^5$ samples the errors are $-0.300$, $+0.005$ and $-0.003$. The optimal standard deviation is $3/\sqrt{N} \approx 0.0095$: the badly scaled step is thirty standard deviations away, while the averaged iterate is within one. Exercise 10 checks the variance 9 over replications.
:::

::: recap
**Key takeaways — chapter 4**

-   Robbins–Monro finds a root of a mean field $h(\theta) = \mathbb{E}[H(\theta, X)]$ from noisy evaluations, with $\sum \gamma_n = \infty$ and $\sum \gamma_n^2 < \infty$.
-   The Robbins–Siegmund lemma turns an almost-supermartingale inequality into almost-sure convergence.
-   With a Lyapunov inequality around a unique root, the iterates converge almost surely; SGD and recursive quantiles are special cases.
-   The ODE method handles several roots, provided the iterates remain bounded.
-   Steps $c/n$ are optimal only if $c$ matches the unknown slope; Polyak–Ruppert averaging with slower steps reaches the optimal covariance $A^{-1}\Gamma A^{-\top}$ automatically.
:::

## 5. Simulation of random variables {#ch5}

Every stochastic algorithm of this course consumes random variables: the samples of SGD, the hidden variables drawn by stochastic EM, the proposals of MCMC, the synthetic data sets of ABC. This chapter builds non-uniform random variables from uniform ones, by inversion, transformation and rejection.

It then introduces importance sampling, which changes the sampling distribution instead of the samples.

### 5.1 Inversion

We assume a generator of independent uniform variables on $(0, 1)$. NumPy's `default_rng` uses the PCG64 generator; the Mersenne Twister (Matsumoto and Nishimura, 1998) is another standard choice.

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Generalised inverse]{.tag} For a distribution function $F$ on $\mathbb{R}$, the generalised inverse is
$$
F^{-}(u) = \inf\{x \in \mathbb{R} : F(x) \ge u\}, \qquad u \in (0, 1).
$$
It coincides with $F^{-1}$ when $F$ is continuous and strictly increasing.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.2 — Inversion]{.tag} If $U$ is uniform on $(0, 1)$, then $F^{-}(U)$ has distribution function $F$.

::: proof
Because $F$ is non-decreasing and right-continuous, $F^{-}(u) \le x$ if and only if $u \le F(x)$. Hence $P(F^{-}(U) \le x) = P(U \le F(x)) = F(x)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Examples follow directly.

-   **Exponential.** $-\log(U)/\lambda$ has law $\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$, since $1 - U$ is uniform too.
-   **Cauchy.** $\tan(\pi(U - 1/2))$ is standard Cauchy.
-   **Discrete laws.** For probabilities $p_1, \dots, p_K$, return the first $k$ with $p_1 + \dots + p_k \ge U$; a binary search on the cumulative sums costs $O(\log K)$ per draw.

Inversion needs $F^{-}$ in closed form or a cheap numerical inverse. The Gaussian distribution function has neither, which motivates the next section.

### 5.2 Transformations

::: prop
[Proposition 5.3 — Box–Muller transform]{.tag} If $U_1$ and $U_2$ are independent and uniform on $(0,1)$, set $R = \sqrt{-2\log U_1}$ and $\Phi = 2\pi U_2$. Then
$$
(R\cos\Phi,\ R\sin\Phi) \text{ is a pair of independent } \mathcal N(0, 1) \text{ variables.}
$$
*Sketch.* In polar coordinates, a standard Gaussian vector of $\mathbb{R}^2$ has an angle uniform on $[0, 2\pi)$, independent of its squared radius. The squared radius follows $\mathrm{Exp}(1/2)$, which inversion generates as $-2\log U_1$.
:::

Two further transformations are used constantly.

-   **Gaussian vectors.** With $\Sigma = LL^\top$ a Cholesky factorisation, $\mu + LZ$ with $Z \sim \mathcal N(0, I_d)$ has law $\mathcal N(\mu, \Sigma)$.
-   **Mixtures, by composition.** Draw the label $z$ from the weights, then $y$ from component $z$. This is how the data of Example 3.8 were generated.

### 5.3 Rejection sampling

::: def
[Algorithm 5.4 — Rejection sampling]{.tag} Let $f$ be a target density known through $\tilde f = Z f$, with $Z > 0$ possibly unknown. Let $g$ be a proposal density that can be sampled, with $\tilde f \le M g$ everywhere. Repeat:

1.  draw $X \sim g$ and $U \sim \mathcal U(0, 1)$ independently;
2.  if $U \le \tilde f(X) / (M g(X))$, return $X$; otherwise start again.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.5 — Correctness and cost of rejection]{.tag} The returned variable has density $f$. The number of proposals $N$ is geometric with success probability $p = Z/M$, so that
$$
\mathbb{E}[N] = \frac{M}{Z} .
$$
When $\tilde f = f$ is normalised, the acceptance rate is $1/M$.

::: proof
For a measurable set $A$, one round accepts a point of $A$ with probability
$$
P(X \in A,\ \text{accept}) = \int_A g(x)\, \frac{\tilde f(x)}{M g(x)}\, dx = \frac{Z}{M} \int_A f(x)\, dx .
$$
With $A = \mathbb{R}^d$, a round succeeds with probability $Z/M$. Dividing, $P(X \in A \mid \text{accept}) = \int_A f$. The rounds are independent, so $N$ is geometric. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 5.6 — A Gaussian from exponentials]{.tag} The half-normal target $f(x) = \sqrt{2/\pi}\, e^{-x^2/2}$ on $x \ge 0$ can be dominated by the proposal $g(x) = e^{-x}$.

-   The ratio $f/g = \sqrt{2/\pi}\, e^{x - x^2/2}$ is maximal at $x = 1$, so the best constant is $M = \sqrt{2e/\pi} \approx 1.3155$.
-   The acceptance probability is $1/M \approx 0.760$, and the test $U \le f(X)/(Mg(X))$ simplifies to $U \le e^{-(X-1)^2/2}$.
-   Attaching an independent random sign gives a standard Gaussian variable.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
M = np.sqrt(2 * np.e / np.pi)                      # sup f/g, attained at x = 1

def half_normal(size):
    out, tried = [], 0
    while sum(len(o) for o in out) < size:
        x = rng.exponential(size=size)             # proposals from g = Exp(1)
        u = rng.random(size)
        out.append(x[u <= np.exp(-0.5 * (x - 1.0) ** 2)])   # accept if U <= f / (M g)
        tried += size
    return np.concatenate(out)[:size], sum(len(o) for o in out) / tried

x, acc = half_normal(200_000)
z = x * rng.choice([-1.0, 1.0], size=x.size)       # random sign -> N(0, 1)
print(f"acceptance {acc:.4f} (1/M = {1 / M:.4f})")
print(f"mean of |Z| {x.mean():.4f} (sqrt(2/pi) = {np.sqrt(2 / np.pi):.4f}),  var of Z {z.var():.4f}")
```

The run prints an acceptance rate of $0.760$, a mean of $|Z|$ equal to $0.799$ (exact value $\sqrt{2/\pi} = 0.798$) and a variance of $Z$ equal to $1.004$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.7 — Rejection degrades exponentially with the dimension]{.tag} For the target $\mathcal N(0, I_d)$ and the proposal $\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 I_d)$ with $\sigma > 1$, the best constant is $M = \sigma^d$. The acceptance rate is therefore $\sigma^{-d}$.

::: proof
The ratio of densities is $\sigma^d \exp\big(-\frac{\|x\|^2}{2}(1 - \sigma^{-2})\big)$, which is maximal at $x = 0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

With a proposal only 10 % wider than the target, in dimension 100, the acceptance rate is
$$
1.1^{-100} \approx 7.3 \times 10^{-5} .
$$
::::

Rejection is therefore a tool for low dimension. In this course it samples full conditionals inside Gibbs samplers (ch. 6), and it is the ancestor of ABC (ch. 9). For log-concave densities in dimension one, adaptive rejection sampling (Gilks and Wild, 1992) builds the envelope automatically from tangents.

### 5.4 Importance sampling

::: def
[Definition 5.8 — Importance sampling]{.tag} Let $g$ be a proposal density that is positive wherever $hf$ is nonzero, and let $w = f/g$ be the importance weight. Then $\mathbb{E}_f[h(X)] = \mathbb{E}_g[h(X) w(X)]$, and with $X_1, \dots, X_n$ independent with density $g$,
$$
\hat I_n^{\mathrm{IS}} = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n h(X_i)\, w(X_i)
$$
is unbiased, with variance $\frac1n\big(\mathbb{E}_g[h^2 w^2] - (\mathbb{E}_f h)^2\big)$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.9 — The optimal proposal]{.tag} Among all proposals, the variance of $\hat I_n^{\mathrm{IS}}$ is minimal for
$$
g^* = \frac{|h|\, f}{\mathbb{E}_f |h|} .
$$
If $h \ge 0$, this proposal gives an estimator with zero variance.

::: proof
By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, $\mathbb{E}_g[h^2 w^2] \ge (\mathbb{E}_g |h| w)^2 = (\mathbb{E}_f |h|)^2$. Equality holds when $|h| w$ is constant, which is the case for $g = g^*$. When $h \ge 0$ the lower bound equals $(\mathbb{E}_f h)^2$ and the variance vanishes. [∎]{.qed}
:::

The optimal proposal involves the unknown integral, so it is never used as such. Its lesson is to put the samples where $|h| f$ is large, not where $f$ is large.
::::

When $f$ is known only up to a constant, the self-normalised estimator
$$
\hat I_n^{\mathrm{SN}} = \frac{\sum_i w(X_i)\, h(X_i)}{\sum_i w(X_i)}
$$
needs only the unnormalised weights. It is consistent, as a ratio of two convergent averages, with a bias of order $1/n$.

The effective sample size $(\sum_i w_i)^2 / \sum_i w_i^2$, between 1 and $n$, is the standard diagnostic of weight degeneracy. ABC-SMC (ch. 9.3) relies on it.

::: ex
[Example 5.10 — A rare event]{.tag} The tail probability $p = P(Z > 4)$ of a standard Gaussian variable equals $3.167 \times 10^{-5}$.

-   Crude Monte Carlo with $n = 10^5$ samples expects $3.2$ hits, so its relative standard error is about $1/\sqrt{np} \approx 0.56$.
-   Importance sampling from $\mathcal N(4, 1)$, a proposal centred on the event, has weight
    $$
    w(y) = \frac{\varphi(y)}{\varphi(y - 4)} = e^{-4y + 8} .
    $$

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
n, p = 100_000, norm.sf(4.0)
naive = rng.standard_normal(n) > 4.0
y = rng.normal(4.0, 1.0, n)                        # proposal N(4, 1)
terms = (y > 4.0) * np.exp(-4.0 * y + 8.0)         # h(y) w(y)
print(f"exact {p:.4e} | naive {naive.mean():.4e} ({naive.sum()} hits) | "
      f"IS {terms.mean():.4e} +/- {1.96 * terms.std() / np.sqrt(n):.1e}")
```

The crude estimate rests on a handful of hits. The importance-sampling estimate has a 95 % half-width close to $4 \times 10^{-7}$, about 1.3 % of $p$, with the same number of samples.
:::

::: recap
**Key takeaways — chapter 5**

-   Inversion: $F^{-}(U) \sim F$; transformations give Gaussians (Box–Muller, Cholesky) and mixtures (composition).
-   Rejection with $\tilde f \le Mg$ is exact and needs on average $M/Z$ proposals per accepted point.
-   Rejection degrades exponentially with the dimension, so it is a low-dimensional tool.
-   Importance sampling reweights samples from $g$; the variance is small when $g$ follows $|h| f$, and the self-normalised version works with unnormalised targets.
-   The effective sample size of the weights detects degeneracy.
:::

## 6. Markov chain Monte Carlo: Metropolis–Hastings and Gibbs {#ch6}

Rejection and importance sampling fail in high dimension because they draw independent points from a fixed proposal, which ignores where the target mass lies. Markov chain Monte Carlo draws dependent points instead. Each point is a local modification of the previous one, accepted or rejected so that the target distribution stays invariant.

This chapter builds the two classical samplers of the syllabus, Metropolis–Hastings and Gibbs, and the theory that justifies their averages.

### 6.1 Markov kernels, invariance and ergodicity

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Kernel, invariance, reversibility]{.tag} A Markov kernel $P(x, A)$ gives, for each state $x$, a probability distribution of the next state. A chain $(X_n)$ with kernel $P$ satisfies $P(X_n \in A \mid \mathcal F_{n-1}) = P(X_{n-1}, A)$.

A distribution $\pi$ is invariant if $\int \pi(dx) P(x, A) = \pi(A)$ for every set $A$. The kernel is reversible with respect to $\pi$, or satisfies detailed balance, if
$$
\pi(dx)\, P(x, dy) = \pi(dy)\, P(y, dx) .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.2 — Detailed balance implies invariance]{.tag} A kernel that is reversible with respect to $\pi$ leaves $\pi$ invariant.

::: proof
Integrate detailed balance over $x$ in the whole space and $y \in A$. The left side gives $\int \pi(dx) P(x, A)$; the right side gives $\int_A \pi(dy) P(y, \mathcal X) = \pi(A)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 6.3 — Irreducibility and aperiodicity]{.tag} A $\pi$-invariant kernel is $\pi$-irreducible if, from every starting point $x$, every set $A$ with $\pi(A) > 0$ is reached with positive probability after some number of steps. It is aperiodic if the state space cannot be split into $k \ge 2$ sets visited cyclically.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 6.4 — Ergodic theorem for MCMC (statement)]{.tag} Let $P$ be $\pi$-invariant, $\pi$-irreducible and aperiodic. Then, for $\pi$-almost every starting point $x$,
$$
\big\| P^n(x, \cdot) - \pi \big\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \longrightarrow 0 .
$$
If the chain is moreover Harris recurrent, then for every starting point and every $h$ integrable under $\pi$, the average $\frac1n \sum_{k \le n} h(X_k)$ converges almost surely to $\pi(h)$.

See Tierney (1994), Meyn and Tweedie (2009), and Douc, Moulines, Priouret and Soulier (2018).
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 6.5 — Central limit theorem for MCMC (statement)]{.tag} If the chain is geometrically ergodic and $\pi(|h|^{2+\delta}) < \infty$ for some $\delta > 0$, then $\sqrt n\,(\hat I_n - \pi(h))$ converges in law to $\mathcal N(0, \sigma_h^2)$, where
$$
\sigma_h^2 = \mathrm{Var}_\pi(h) \Big(1 + 2 \sum_{k \ge 1} \rho_k\Big) = \mathrm{Var}_\pi(h)\, \tau_h ,
$$
$\rho_k$ is the lag-$k$ autocorrelation of $h(X_n)$ at stationarity, and $\tau_h$ is the integrated autocorrelation time.
:::

A chain of length $n$ is worth $n/\tau_h$ independent samples: this is its effective sample size (ESS). Positive autocorrelations make $\tau_h > 1$, and every sampler below is judged by this number.

### 6.2 The Metropolis–Hastings algorithm

::: def
[Algorithm 6.6 — Metropolis–Hastings (Metropolis et al., 1953; Hastings, 1970)]{.tag} The target $\pi$ is known through an unnormalised density $\tilde\pi$. A proposal kernel has density $q(x, y)$. From $X_{n-1} = x$:

1.  draw a candidate $Y \sim q(x, \cdot)$;
2.  accept it with probability
    $$
    \alpha(x, y) = \min\Big(1,\ \frac{\tilde\pi(y)\, q(y, x)}{\tilde\pi(x)\, q(x, y)}\Big) ;
    $$
3.  set $X_n = Y$ if it is accepted, and $X_n = x$ otherwise.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.7 — Metropolis–Hastings is reversible]{.tag} The kernel of Algorithm 6.6 satisfies detailed balance with respect to $\pi$, hence leaves $\pi$ invariant. The normalising constant of $\pi$ is never needed.

::: proof
